newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-ELS'S OPEN VICTORY IS A FAMILY AFFAIR.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-ELS'S OPEN VICTORY IS A FAMILY AFFAIR.

text.p: Ernie Els's second U.S. Open victory was a family affair -- as golf has always been for the 27-year-old South African.

Els, whose parents were here to witness his triumph, said Sunday that he drew inspiration for his victory from his mother's 89-year-old father, who introduced the Els family to golf about the time he was born.

The broad-shouldered, soft-spoken Els said that a Saturday night telephone conversation he had with his grandfather back in South Africa was just what he needed to survive the pressure-packed final day of the Open.

"I just felt like I wanted to speak to him. I had to talk to him. He's such a wise man," Els said of the long-distance conversation with his namesake. "I had a good feeling after that. I had him in my thoughts all day."

It was amazing that Els could think at all during the tumultuous finale -- a see-saw, four-way battle which included Tom Lehman, Colin Montgomerie and Jeff Maggert that was not decided until the final hole.
Els, who shot a one-under-par 69 to prevail by one stroke over Montgomerie, said that his grandfather, Ernie Vernaak, had alays been very special to him.
"He played a big part in my life," Els said. "He got my dad interested in golf and he got me and my brother interested."
Els's father, Cornelius, a single-digit handicapper, said, however, that Ernie was a natural at both golf and tennis, winning international junior events in both sports.
"He was born to be a sportsman," the proud father said just after he and his wife watched their son become the first non-American in 87 years to win two U.S. Opens.
"It comes natural to him," the elder Els said of his son's apparent ability to remain calm under the most trying circumstances.

"Maybe my exterior is calm," the newly crowned champion said of his demeanor during his four-way battle on Congressional Country Club's grassy torture chamber, which got the best of many of the world's elite golfers.
"I was quite intense," he admitted. "But I had confidence in myself and my game. I felt comfortable. I had the will to push it through."

In addition to the inspiration he got from his grandfather, Els also drew upon his experience -- especially his victory in the 1994 U.S. Open, which he won in an 18-hole, three-way playoff that included Montgomerie.
"I've played in a lot of major championships the last four or five years and I think that with experience you become a little bit more calm," he said. "You have to be calm to win major tournaments.
"Three years ago when I won this tournament it was like a war out there. I knew it was going to be the same today."

He was right. There was a four-way tie, two three-way ties and three different individual leaders during the first nine alone. Then two more times on the back nine all four players were again knotted atop the leaderboard.
"It must have been one hell of a show on television," Els said.
But maybe it was Els's desire to put on a show of his own that led to his stirring victory, which came on Father's Day, an unofficial holiday in the United States.
"My mom and dad were here," Els said with the sparkling Open trophy sitting in front of him. "I wanted to show off a litle bit and show them how to win a U.S. Open."
It was indeed a family affair.
